IX. Pulmonary Gas  Exchange
Learning objectives:
P29. Name the factors that affect diffusive transport of a gas between
alveolar gas and pulmonary capillary blood (Fick’s Law).
P30. Describe the kinetics of oxygen transfer from alveolus to capillary and 
the concept of capillary reserve time (i.e., the portion of the erythrocyte 
transit time in which no further diffusion of oxygen occurs). 
P31. Calculate diffusing capacity from carbon monoxide uptake and carbon 
monoxide partial pressure. 
P32. Contrast the uptake of O2, CO, and N2O from the lungs to pulmonary 
capillary blood. 
P33. Describe why normal subjects at high altitude or patients with lung 
disease may have a diffusion limitation during exercise.  
I.  Introduction  
The exchange of O2 and CO2 between the air and blood & between blood and
tissues occurs by the process of diffusion. This is a passive process that does
not involve any type of active transport of oxygen across the tissues that
separate alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood.
The lung structure is well suited to high rates of diffusion.
At rest, the
pulmonary capillary volume of 75 ml is spread over an area of roughly 90 m2.
Since stroke volume of the right ventricle is also about 75 ml, the pulmonary
capillaries are refilled every time the heart beats. This lecture will cover:
1) the air-blood barrier and factors that determine the rate of diffusion of O2
and CO2
2) diffusing capacity
3) the kinetics of O2 transfer into pulmonary capillaries
4) diffusion and perfusion limitation.

II.  Air-Blood  Barrier      
Pulmonary capillary blood is separated from alveolar gas by the “air-blood barrier”. Under
normal conditions, this is not really much of a barrier, as gas diffuses easily and rapidly
across it. Passive diffusion is the process that drives oxygen into the capillary blood and
carbon dioxide out of pulmonary capillary blood.
The following figure shows the
components of the air-blood barrier. After oxygen gets through the barrier, it must also
diffuse through plasma and into the red blood cell.
Parts of the air blood barrier include:
1) alveolar epithelium
2) tissue interstitium
3) capillary endothelium
4) plasma layer
5) red cell membrane
6) red cell cytoplasm
7) gas binding to hemoglobin
For most of the lung, the barrier is very thin, in average about 0.3 - 1 μm. As shown above,
the red cell may be some distance from the capillary endothelium. After entering the
red cell, oxygen combines with hemoglobin. This diffusion and chemical reaction add to
the time needed for a complete diffusion.

III.
Diffusion process (Fick’s
law):
Passive diffusion proceeds at a rate (Vgas)
proportional to the driving force (P1 – P2), surface area (A), diffusion coefficient (d) and
solubility of the diffusing gas (α) and inversely proportional to thickness of the barrier (T).
These factors comprise Fick’s law for passive diffusion, where (d ∙α) is Krogh’s diffusion
constant (K). However, area and thickness of the membrane (geometrical properties of
the gas exchange surface) can not be measured accurately. Therefore, these factors
along with K (= d ∙α) are lumped to form a parameter called diffusing capacity (DL):
DL = d ∙α ∙ A/T
Using diffusing capacity in the fick’s law: 
Vgas = DL ∙(P1 – P2)
This equation for the gas diffusion rate can be rearranged to provide the equation for 
diffusing capacity: 
DL = Vgas / (P1 – P2)
The lung diffusing capacity is different for individual gases like O2, CO2 and N2, because
the solubility α (a component of D) is different for these gases. Diffusing capacity for CO2
(DLCO2) is 20 times greater than Diffusing capacity for O2 (DLO2).
DLCO2 = 20 ∙DLO2
Therefore, Diffusion problems in a diseased lung may affect the oxygen transfer from
alveolar gas into the capillary blood but not the CO2 transfer from the blood into the
alveolar space.

IV. How can DLO2 be measured?
Applying the equation of diffusion capacity for O2 reveals that lung diffusing capacity
for O2 can be determined by:
DLO2 = VO2/(PAO2 – PC'O2)
Whereby VO2 is O2 uptake, PAO2 is alveolar PO2 and PC'O2 is the pulmonary capillary
PO2. However, the pulmonary capillary PO2 is not constant and changes from 40
mmHg at the entrance of the capillary to 100 mmHg at the end of the capillary.
Therefore, it is difficult to average the value for the use in above equation. However,
it is common today to measure the lung diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
(DLCO) instead of DLO2. CO is used in a very small concentration for this
measurement. Because of a very high affinity of hemoglobin for CO, nearly all CO
molecules bind with hemoglobin and thus CO partial pressure in the capillary blood
remains zero. It simplifies the measurement of DLCO as far as only CO uptake and
alveolar PCO are needed to be measured:
DLCO = VCO/(PACO – PC'CO)
Because PC'CO = 0, Then
DLCO = VCO/PACO
DLCO and DLO2 differ from one another only by a constant factor (due to a constant
difference between αO2 and αCO), so that DLO2 can be estimated from DLCO.

V. Factors  that  change  Diffusing  Capacity (DL)  
A. Body Position: Diffusing capacity is higher in the supine position due to 
increased pulmonary capillary volume and more even distribution of pulmonary 
blood flow (both increasing gas exchange surface area).   
B. Body Size: Lung size is an important predictor of DL due to the direct 
relationship between lung size and surface area. Lung size and lung volume 
(VL) are also proportional. Therefore, DL is related to VL as well. However, the 
ratio DL/VL is normally used to become independent of lung size or body size. 
C. Exercise: Increased cardiac output during exercise results in recruitment 
and distension of pulmonary capillaries and also better ventilation/perfusion 
matching. This results in increased surface area and is beneficial for DL. 
However, the increased cardiac output shortens the transit time (time available 
for diffusion) and can result in incomplete transfer of oxygen; i.e., a diffusion 
limitation.  This does not occur in normal, healthy individuals but can occur in 
elite athletes at maximal exercise where capillary transit time is extremely 
reduced by their extra-large  cardiac output.

VI. Pathological factors that influence Diffusing Capacity
Any pathological condition that increases thickness or decreases surface area
of the alveolar-capillary membrane such as decreased capillary blood volume
or attenuated pulmonary blood pressure will decrease diffusing capacity.
Examples are obstructive lung disease (emphysema), cystic fibrosis, interstitial
lung disease (fibrosis), left heart failure leading to pulmonary edema, and
pneumonia.

VII. Kinetic of O2 transfer into pulmonary capillary blood
Driving force for O2 diffusion from alveolar gas into the capillary blood (PA -
PC')O2 is the highest at the beginning of the capillary. Therefore, a significant
amount of O2 enters the blood at the initial segments of the capillary. This O2
transfer causes PO2 to continually rise and leads to a reduction of driving
pressure for further O2 diffusion in the subsequent parts of the capillary (see
figure). The result is a continuous reduction of O2 uptake along the length of
capillary. A complete equilibrium between alveolar gas and capillary blood is
finally reached towards the end of the capillary, and consequently both alveolar
gas and the blood leaving the capillary have the same PO2 and PCO2.
Transit time of the blood in the lung capillary is in average one second, but a
complete equilibration between gas and blood occurs in much less than one
second (approximately 1/4 - 1/3 of a sec). This is because the lung diffusing
capacity is so high that the air-blood barrier at rest cannot oppose a significant
diffusion resistance for O2 or CO2.

VIII.  Limitation  of  Gas  Transfer  
A. Diffusion Limitation
Diffusion limitation is defined as an incomplete equilibration of O2 partial
pressure between alveolar gas and capillary blood. As a result arterial PO2
remains below alveolar PO2 and an alveolar-arterial PO2 difference (A-a)PO2
develops. However, there will be no diffusion limitation for CO2 even if O2
transfer is limited by diffusion (CO2 diffusing capacity is 20 times higher than
DLO2). In the following slides some physiological parameters are discussed
that could possibly produce a diffusion limitation for oxygen.

1. Exercise: During exercise cardiac output increases much more than
pulmonary capillary volume increases.
This imbalance between the two
shortens blood transit time through lung capillaries. In healthy subjects,
however, there is no diffusion limitation during exercise at sea level. In elite
athletes maximum cardiac output may reach 50 L/min.
In this case, transit
time gets reduced so much that equilibration does not occur and the athlete
develops arterial hypoxemia due to this diffusion limitation.
2. Low DL caused by decreased surface area or increased thickness can
create a diffusion limitation.
Patients with lung damage or disease that
decreased DL may be normal at rest but become short of breath with exercise.
The reason for this is reduction of transit time which “unmasks” their diffusion
limitation.

3. Low alveolar PO2 (hypoxia): During mild hypoxia no significant diffusion
limitation (incomplete equilibration) may occur for O2. However, in deep
hypoxia or by combination of hypoxia with exercise (for example exercise at
high altitude) a significant diffusion limitation for O2 is likely to occur even in a
normal lung. This is primarily related to the shape of O2 dissociation curve that
has a steep slope in the hypoxic region. This implies that adding a significant
amount of O2 into the blood will be associated only with a very small change in
PO2. Therefore, the rapid rise in blood PO2 that occurs by O2 transfer in a

Consequently, capillary blood PO2 can not reach equilibrium with alveolar PO2
and remains below the alveolar level even at the end of the capillary. This
inequality is called alveolar-end capillary PO2 difference (A - C')PO2.
The alveolar PO2 in the graph (50 mm Hg) is normal at 20,000 feet above sea
level (e.g., summit of Mt. McKinley in Alaska). Climbers near the summit would
have a significant diffusion limitation and widened (A – a)PO2 while exercising.
Please be aware that the diffusing capacity for CO2 is so large that CO2
transfer from capillary blood into the alveolar gas never becomes diffusion
limited, not even in a diseased lung.

B. Perfusion Limitation
O2 uptake is normally complete within 0.25 sec and is not limited by diffusion.
Once the transfer of O2 is complete, then O2 diffusion into that volume of blood
stops. The only way to transfer more O2 would be to add more blood; i.e.,
increase flow. This means that O2 transfer is normally perfusion limited. The
only way O2 transfer becomes diffusion limited is with lung disease or high
altitude.

N2O is perfusion limited:
Nitrous oxide is highly soluble in blood and is rapidly taken up by pulmonary
capillary blood when a patient has inhaled nitrous oxide. Its uptake rate is not
diffusion limited, because its partial pressure in the blood equilibrates so
quickly with its partial pressure in the alveolar gas. The only way additional
uptake can occur is by increased perfusion (Perfusion limited).

CO is diffusion limited:
Carbon monoxide, on the other hand, creates almost no back pressure in the
pulmonary capillaries (used at a very low concentration) because this gas is
mopped up almost completely by hemoglobin. Therefore, the rate of transfer
of CO is limited almost entirely by diffusing properties of the lung (area and
distance) and not by blood flow. It is this property of CO that makes it the ideal
gas for measuring diffusing capacity. The only way to transfer more CO is to
have thinner barrier or more surface area.

Summary: Oxygen is transferred much more slowly than nitrous oxide but fast
enough so that there is normally no diffusion limitation; i.e., equilibration is
complete prior to blood leaving the pulmonary capillary. The only way to
enhance O2 transport is to increase pulmonary blood flow, and, therefore, O2
transport is normally perfusion limited. The only way O2 transfer becomes
diffusion limited is with lung disease or high altitude.
CO always has a diffusion limitation because the partial pressure in capillary
blood stays very low due to rapid combination with hemoglobin.
You can use the equation for gas transfer to understand diffusion limitation
versus perfusion limitation: Vgas = DL x (P1-P2). For CO, P2 = 0 and P1 is
constant. Therefore, the only way to increase Vgas would be to increase DL
(diffusion limited). For N2O, P1-P2 rapidly becomes zero, so Vgas stops. The
only way to increase Vgas would be to add new blood to the capillaries
(perfusion limited).

IX. Gas Diffusion in Body Tissues: The final step of O2 uptake (and the first step of CO2 release) is diffusion between blood
and tissues. The role of hemoglobin is to deliver enough oxygen at a high partial pressure for an adequate diffusion of O2 into the
tissue.
Like in the lung, the morphological factors of surface area and diffusion distance are very important in tissues, where diffusion
distance depends on capillary density.
Capillary density is adaptive to muscle function.
For example, cardiac muscle contains 3,000 to 4,000 capillaries per mm2
compared to 300 to 500 per mm2 for skeletal muscle. If oxygen delivery is inadequate to maintain an adequate rate of oxygen
diffusion, tissue death (infarction) occurs. In contrast to the lung where O2 transfer occurs per simple diffusion, it is facilitated in
skeletal muscle by myoglobin, which also acts as a high affinity O2 store.
The amount of myoglobin is highly variable and
correlated with the aerobic capacity of the muscle. An example is shown in the figure comparing Mahi Mahi muscle (white, low
myoglobin) with that of tuna (dark, high myoglobin).
SUMMARY
1. The air-blood barrier includes all of the membranes. Its properties of surface area and thickness influence the rate of diffusion
of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Reaction rate with hemoglobin is equally important in determining the rate of diffusion
2. Diffusing capacity (DL) is the transfer rate of a gas in ml/minute per mm Hg driving pressure; i.e., DL = flow/ΔP. DL goes up
during exercise due to recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries.
3. DL has units of flow/driving pressure. It is a conductance (reciprocal of resistance). The variables of DL include surface area,
distance, characteristics of the gas (solubility and molecular weight), [Hb] concentration, and capillary volume.
4. The rate of equilibration during passage through the pulmonary capillary is fastest for N2O (nitrous oxide), which is considered
perfusion limited. Next fastest is oxygen (also normally perfusion limited). Equilibration never occurs for carbon monoxide, which
is diffusion limited and therefore used as a test gas to measure diffusing capacity.
5. The length of time (transit time) available for gas transfer in the pulmonary capillaries is based on cardiac output. At rest, stoke
volume is roughly equal to pulmonary capillary volume.
Therefore, each time the heart beats, pulmonary capillary volume is
replaced.
6. The change in PO2 as a function of time in the pulmonary capillary blood is determined by the driving pressure (more pressure =
steeper slope) and membrane properties (higher DL = steeper slope). A shortened transit time (e.g., increased cardiac output)
may result in diffusion limitation (= incomplete equilibration) for abnormal lungs and for normal lungs at high altitude.

KEY CONCEPTS
1. Fick's law states that the rate of diffusion of a gas 
through a tissue sheet is proportional to the area of 
the sheet and the partial pressure difference across it, 
and inversely proportional to the thickness of the 
sheet. 
2. Examples of diffusion- and perfusion-limited gases 
are carbon monoxide and nitrous oxide, respectively. 
Oxygen transfer is normally perfusion limited, but 
some diffusion limitation may occur under some 
conditions, including intense exercise, thickening of 
the blood-gas barrier, and alveolar hypoxia. 
3. The diffusing capacity of the lung is measured using 
inhaled carbon monoxide. The value increases 
markedly on exercise. 
4. Carbon dioxide transfer into the blood is probably not 
diffusion limited.

Pulmonary circulation
The lung is the organ with the highest blood perfusion in the body as total cardiac output is
streaming through the lung. The low driving pressure difference (pressure in right ventricle
minus pressure in left atrium) reveals that Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) is much
less than total peripheral resistance (TPR) of the systemic circulation (see the figure). At
rest, PVR is 16 times less than TPR.
The intravascular pressures in pulmonary circulation (unlike systemic circulation) are very
low, and therefore, pulmonary blood flow is strongly affected by the hydrostatic (gravity)
forces as well as by perivacular pressures.
Related to perivascular pressures we can differentiate three vascular sections in pulmonary
circulation:
1. Large extra pulmonary vessels that are lying with the heart and cava veins in the
mediastinum. Pressure in mediastinum equals pleural pressure (Ppl), which is normally
negative. Therefore, these vessels are pulled outwards by this negative pressure and
remain open. During inspiration the pleural pressure becomes even more negative, and
the vessels get dilated which in turn supports the blood flow.
2. The arteries and veins that are branching together with the bronchial system. These
vessels (like bronchi themselves) are surrounded by the lung tissue with its recoiling
force. The perivascular pressure of these vessels is the same as pleural pressure.
3. The alveolar capillaries that are lying within alveolar walls of neighboring alveoli are
surrounded by alveolar pressure.

Left Atrial Pressure is Measured via a Pulmonary Artery
Pulmonary artery balloon catheters (Swan-Ganz ) can be used to measure
pulmonary artery pressure as well as left atrial pressure. Once the catheter is
advanced into the pulmonary artery, the pressure (pulmonary artery) can be
measured before the balloon is inflated. After the balloon is inflated there is no
blood flow and thus the pressure measured at the tip of the catheter equals the
left atrial pressure (wedge pressure). This is used clinically to diagnose mitral
stenosis or congestive heart failure.

Control of Pulmonary Vascular Resistance 
(PVR)
Cardiac output
Mechanisms
Pulmonary vascular resistance
The low inside pressure (pulmonary blood pressure) and the outside
perivascular pressure (= pleural pressure for most of the lung vessels)
determine the diameter of vessels and, thus PVR in the lung. As mentioned
above PVR is normally very low in comparison to TPR.
Exercise causes cardiac output and thus, lung perfusion to increase by 3 to 6
fold of their levels at rest. The pressure in pulmonary artery, however,
increases much less, maximally by factor 2. Since the driving pressure
difference increases much less than perfusion, the PVR has to be reduced.
Passive and active forces are involved in determination of the PVR.
Passive forces affecting PVR
A decrease in PVR is caused either by widening of already perfused vessels
or by opening of closed vessels (Recruitment). Both of these processes are
passive and occur as cardiac output is increasing during exercise.
Pulmonary blood pressure affects PVR: Increases in intravascular (blood)
pressure in the pulmonary arteries as well as in pulmonary veins stretch the
pulmonary vessels and leads to decreases in PVR.
H. Shams

Lung volume affects PVR: Increasing lung volume elevates the recoiling
force of the lung which in turn stretches and distends extraalveolar arterial
and venous vessels. Therefore, the resistance of these vessels decreases as
lung volume increases. At the same time, lung inflation also causes elongation
and compression of capillaries within alveolar walls, so-called alveolar
vessels and their resistance increases.
The resistances of both alveolar and extraalveolar vessels are in series and
therefore additive. This leads to lowest total PVR at FRC and to an increased
PVR (decreased flow) with either lung inflation or deflation from FRC (see
figure).

Active forces affecting PVR
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: Hypoxia acts directly on pulmonary
vascular smooth muscle to increase PVR. The smaller pulmonary vessels constrict
when local alveolar PO2 falls. This constriction is augmented if alveolar PCO2 rises.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction is a response to a decrease of PO2 in alveolar gas, not in
the blood, causing hypoxic vasoconstriction only in those regions that are hypoxic.
This regional hypoxic vasoconstriction is beneficial for the efficiency of gas
exchange. When alveolar ventilation is decreased by an obstructed airway or other
injury, local hypoxic vasoconstriction reduces the blood flow to this hypoxic region,
and the blood is directed to a region with higher ventilation. Thus, the perfusion of
the hypoxic region is adjusted to match its low ventilation, and its gas exchange
remains near normal.
Global hypoxia is however considered a disadvantage. Patients with generalized
alveolar hypoxia due to lung disease or low PIO2 (high altitude) may develop
pulmonary hypertension and eventually right heart failure. At high altitude, some
normal individuals develop high altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), possibly
because of a greater hypoxic vasoconstriction response that causes pulmonary
hypertension (see figure).

Hypoxia is believed to inhibit a K+ channel in the membrane of smooth muscle cells of
pulmonary vessels. This inhibition of K+ channel depolarizes the cell membrane and opens
the voltage gated Ca++ channels, through which Ca++ enters the cells and causes
contraction. Hypoxia also leads to the release of endothelin-1 from the endothelial cells
causing contraction of smooth muscles.
This effect of hypoxia in pulmonary circulation is opposite to what is seen in the systemic
circulation where low oxygen produces vasodilatation that is mediated through an ATP
dependent K+ channel (Hypoxia opens this channel and produces hyperpolarization of the
cells). In the systemic circulation, hypoxia also causes endothelium to release nitric oxide
(NO) which dilates the vessels.
Pulmonary vascular resistance can also be affected by a number of vaso-active
substances like histamine, serotonin, angiotensin II, prostaglandins and nitric oxide (NO).
In a healthy person, all these substances may modify PVR, but are not involved in the
process of hypoxic vasoconstriction. NO is however, clinically used in pulmonary failure
(ARDS) to reduce PVR and improve gas exchange.
Autonomic control is not important in pulmonary circulation
Although sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves are present in the lungs, the autonomic
nervous system exerts little or no control over pulmonary circulation in humans. However,
pulmonary vascular resistance is altered by vasoactive drugs; e.g., beta 2 agonists, used to
treat asthma, cause bronchodilatation.

Reflexes reducing VA/Q mismatch: Lets assume we have a mismatch of ventilation
and perfusion in the lungs with alveolar region 1 receiving a high ventilation and a low
perfusion, and alveolar region 2 receiving a low ventilation and a high perfusion. It is
obvious that region 1 is relatively hyperventilated and becomes hyperoxic and
hypocapnic. In contrary, region 2 is relatively hypoventilated and becomes hypoxic and
hypercapnic. The resulting hypocapnia and hypoxia activate reflexes, which reduce the
magnitude of these VA/Q inhomogeneities. Hypocapnia of region 1 causes bronchi of
region 1 to constrict (hypocapnic bronchoconstriction), and thus enhances the airway
resistance in region 1, reduces its airflow by diverting part of it to region 2. As a result,
the airflow in region 1 decreases and in region 2 increases and thus flow of both regions
becomes similar. On the blood side, alveolar hypoxia of region 2 causes the blood
vessels in region 2 to constrict (hypoxic vasoconstriction) and reduces its blood flow by
diverting part of the blood flow from region 2 to region 1. Therefore, this reflex corrects
the uneven blood flow to both regions and make them similar. In summary, both reflexes
hypocapnic bronchoconstriction and hypoxic vasoconstriction are powerful mechanisms
to reduce the magnitude of an uneven VA/Q inhomogeneity.

Distribution of blood flow in the lung.
The gravity force causes blood pressure to be lower at the top than at the
lower areas of lungs (see figure). In an upright body position some lung
regions close to the peak may have capillary blood pressures lower than
alveolar pressure (PA). These capillaries will be compressed by PAand will not
be perfused with blood (zone I). On the other hand, capillaries at the base of
the lung, where both pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary venous
pressure are higher than PA, will be permanently perfused (zone 3). In the
middle zone (zone II), where PA is lower than arterial but higher than venous
pressure, the capillary will be slightly compressed at a point towards end of the
capillary and remains perfused at a lower range. Therefore, the perfusion of
the lung is unequally distributed, particularly in the upright position. The
perfusion increases from the peak to the base of the lung. This regional
unequal distribution of blood flow affects the efficiency of the pulmonary gas
exchange (more later).The increase in pulmonary artery pressure during
exercise minimizes zone I and reduces the inequality of distribution.

Bronchial circulation: Bronchial artery blood is oxygenated blood that
supplies the supporting tissues of the lungs, including the connective tissue,
septa, and large and small bronchi. A small fraction of the bronchial venous
blood (deoxygenated blood) drains into the pulmonary veins and enters the left
atrium, producing a shunt of deoxygenated into oxygenated blood. The major
fraction of bronchial venous blood drains into Azygos- and hemiazygos veins.
Coronary circulation: Coronary venous blood (deoxygenated blood) partially
enters the left atrium and left ventricle via Thebesian veins
(venae cordis
minimae) and is the second normal source of venous admixture or shunt.
These shunts are only about 1 to 2 per cent of the total cardiac output and
contribute about equally with VA/Q mismatch for the normal alveolar-arterial
PO2 difference of 3-10 mm Hg. The human fetus has additional normal shunts;
i.e., the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus.

Congenital or pathological conditions, such as pulmonary arteriovenous
fistulas produce shunts in which venous blood is added to arterial blood (right
to left, or R →L shunts).
Intracardiac defects may produce R →L or L →R shunts depending on the
pressures of the two connected chambers. A right to left shunt is harmful by
adding deoxygenated blood to arterialized blood and lowering the oxygen of
blood going to tissues. A left to right shunt is harmful by increasing pulmonary
artery pressure and possibly causing hypoxemia by increasing perfusion and
lowering V/Q ratios in the lung. Left to right shunt is detected by a finding of
abnormally high oxygen saturation in the right atrium or ventricle.

Fluid Exchange in Pulmonary Capillaries
The Starling forces you learned about for systemic capillaries are qualitatively the same in the pulmonary circulation, but two additional forces are
important in the lungs: alveolar pressure and surface tension. Pulmonary edema (excess fluid in the interstitial space or alveoli) can result from
increased capillary permeability or from increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased colloid osmotic pressure in the capillary. Increased surface tension
in the alveoli (surfactant deficiency) would also cause edema.
Pulmonary Edema has multiple Causes
1) Increased hydrostatic pressure.
Mitral stenosis and congestive heart failure result in increased left atrial and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic
pressure. The lymphatic system of the lung has a high capacity to remove excess filtered fluid (“lymphatic reserve”), so that edema start to form after
left atrial pressure is elevated to above 20 mm Hg. This type of edema is called “cardiogenic edema”.
2)
Increased
permeability.
Damage to capillary and alveolar endothelium allows plasma proteins to leak into the interstitial space and alveoli.
Water then moves into the interstitial space and alveoli by osmosis. Inflammation and heroin overdose are two examples of factors causing this type of
edema. This type of edema is called “non-cardiogenic edema”.
3) High surface tension. If surfactant is reduced, surface tension will increase leading to fluid movement into the interstitial space and alveoli. Acute
respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is associated with both an increase capillary permeability and decreased surfactant.
Both factors result in
pulmonary edema.
4) Decreased plasma protein.
Decreased colloid osmotic pressure can also result in pulmonary (as well as systemic; e.g., ascites) edema.
(Examples: starvation, liver disease, hemodilution ).
5) Impaired lymphatic drainage or increased central venous pressure. In the lung, if the lymphatic vessels are blocked or lymph drainage flow
back to the central veins is impeded by high central venous pressure, edema will result (examples; cancer, heart failure).
6) High altitude pulmonary edema.
Global hypoxia as observed by pulmonary diseases like COPD or at high altitude leads to pulmonary
hypertension. In COPD, hypertension often leads to right heart failure (Cor Pulmonale). A small percentage of normal subjects at high altitude develop
pulmonary edema (HAPE) but the mechanism is not clear.
Lung fluid collected from HAPE patients has elevated protein levels indicating a non-
cardiogenic cause (inflammatory response).
7) Drowning. Freshwater and saltwater drowning both fills the lungs with water (unless the victim has a laryngospasm). Freshwater rapidly enters the
pulmonary circulation and causes hemodilution that results in a decreased plasma osmolarity. The red blood cells rupture and release potassium, which
in turn leads to death by ventricular fibrillation and asphyxiation.
Salt water is hypertonic and leads to water loss from blood into lungs.
Death is
occurring by asphyxiation.
Pleural Effusion
Pleural effusion is edema of the pleural space. At FRC, pressure in pleural space is negative (about – 4 mm Hg), due to tendency of lungs to collapse
and chest wall to spring out. However, pleural space between visceral and parietal pleura is filled with a tiny layer of fluid. The amount of the fluid is
regulated by capillaries located on surfaces of both visceral- and parietal pleura. Fluid accumulation in this space is called Pleural effusion. X-ray shows
blunting of the costophrenic angle (where ribs meet diaphragm) by pleural effusion. The base of the lung is always more susceptible to edema because
of the higher hydrostatic pressure at the base.

KEY CONCEPTS
1.
The pressures within the pulmonary circulation are much lower 
than in the systemic circulation. Also the capillaries are exposed to 
alveolar pressure, whereas the pressures around the extra-alveolar 
vessels are lower. 
2.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is low and falls even more when 
cardiac output increases because of recruitment and distension of 
the capillaries. Pulmonary vascular resistance increases at very 
low or high lung volumes. 
3.
Blood flow is unevenly distributed in the upright lung. There is a 
much higher flow at the base than the apex as a result of gravity. If 
capillary pressure is less than alveolar pressure at the top of the 
lung, the capillaries collapse and there is no blood flow (zone 1). 
4.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction reduces the blood flow to 
poorly ventilated regions of the lung. Release of this mechanism is 
responsible for a large increase in blood flow to the lung at birth. 
5.
Fluid movement across the capillary endothelium is governed by 
the Starling equilibrium. 
6.
The pulmonary circulation has many metabolic functions, notably 
the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II by angiotensin-
converting enzyme.
